questions.question: Why does changing a plain `var` inside a composable not update the UI, while changing a mutableStateOf value does?
options: Plain vars are copied into the UI once at compile time
Its reads and writes are tracked by the snapshot system
Plain vars can only be changed on a background thread
mutableStateOf forces a full Activity redraw on every change
questions.explanation: Compose can only react to what it can observe: reads of snapshot state are recorded against the reading scope, and writes notify those scopes. A plain var is invisible to the runtime and is also re-initialised on recomposition unless remembered.

questions.question: Calling `list.value.add(item)` on a `mutableStateOf(mutableListOf<Item>())` triggers recomposition of composables that read `list.value`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Only assigning `.value` counts as a snapshot write; mutating the object inside doesn't. Either assign a new list (`list.value = list.value + item`) or use mutableStateListOf, whose operations are snapshot-aware.

questions.question: What are the two printed values A and B?
questions.code:
val state = mutableStateOf(1)
val snap = Snapshot.takeMutableSnapshot()
snap.enter { state.value = 2 }
println(state.value) // A
snap.apply()
println(state.value) // B
snap.dispose()
questions.explanation: Writes made inside a mutable snapshot are isolated until it is applied, so code outside still sees 1. apply() publishes the changes, after which reads see 2. This isolation is what lets composition run without exposing half-finished state.

questions.question: `state` holds a data class. Code runs `state.value = state.value.copy()` without changing any field. With the default mutableStateOf, what happens?
options: Readers recompose, because copy() returns a new instance
Nothing is invalidated, since the new value equals the old one
It throws, since copy() of the current value is a no-op write
Readers recompose twice, once for the read and once for the write
questions.explanation: mutableStateOf defaults to structuralEqualityPolicy, so a write that is == to the current value is not treated as a change. referentialEqualityPolicy would notify on any new instance. This is one reason data classes with proper equals work well as state.

questions.question: Reading which of these inside a composable will cause recomposition when it changes, with no extra conversion? Select all that apply.
options: A list created with mutableStateListOf
A MutableStateFlow's value property
A map created with mutableStateMapOf
The value of a derivedStateOf
An ArrayList held in a remember
questions.explanation: SnapshotStateList/Map and derived state are snapshot objects, so reads are tracked. A StateFlow is not snapshot state; reading .value is a one-off read that won't recompose, so it needs collectAsState/collectAsStateWithLifecycle. A plain ArrayList is invisible to Compose.

questions.question: How does the runtime know which state objects a composable read during composition?
options: The compiler lists every state a function references in its bytecode
It compares every state value before and after each frame is drawn
Composition runs in a snapshot whose read observer records each read
Every State holds a strong list of composables, added at declaration
questions.explanation: The Recomposer composes inside a mutable snapshot with a read observer; each state read calls it, and the runtime links that object to the current recompose scope. Static analysis can't know which branches run, and diffing every value each frame would be far too expensive.

questions.question: Composition runs inside a mutable snapshot, so state writes made during composition are not visible to other threads until that snapshot is applied.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The Recomposer takes a mutable snapshot for each composition pass and applies it when the pass succeeds. Writes inside are isolated until then, and if the pass is abandoned they're discarded. That is part of why side effects belong in effect APIs.

questions.question: Two mutable snapshots write different values to the same state, then both are applied. With the default policy, what are `ra` and `rb`?
questions.code:
val s = mutableStateOf(0)
val a = Snapshot.takeMutableSnapshot()
val b = Snapshot.takeMutableSnapshot()
a.enter { s.value = 1 }
b.enter { s.value = 2 }
val ra = a.apply()
val rb = b.apply()
options: Both succeed, and the state ends up holding 2 since b applied last
Both fail, since neither snapshot saw the other's write
ra succeeds; rb fails because the policy can't merge the write
ra fails and rb succeeds, as the newest snapshot always wins
questions.explanation: The first apply succeeds. The second finds the state changed since b was taken, so it asks the mutation policy to merge; structuralEqualityPolicy can't merge 1 and 2, so b's apply returns a Failure. Custom policies can override merge to resolve such conflicts.

questions.question: Which statements about SnapshotStateObserver are true? Select all that apply.
options: It re-runs the observed block automatically every time a read state changes
Compose UI uses it to track state reads during layout and draw
observeReads records the state objects read inside the given block for a scope
It relies on snapshot apply notifications to learn which objects changed
questions.explanation: SnapshotStateObserver ties reads to a scope and, when an apply notification includes one of those objects, calls the onChanged callback for that scope. It doesn't re-run your block; the caller decides what to do, such as requesting re-layout or redraw. Compose UI uses it so layout and draw reads don't need recomposition.

questions.question: What does snapshotFlow { pagerState.currentPage } give you?
options: A hot SharedFlow that replays every page change to new collectors
A cold Flow that emits whenever the result of the block changes
A State that can be read directly in a composable
A Flow that emits once per frame whether or not the page changed
questions.explanation: snapshotFlow runs the block, records the state it read, and re-runs it when those states change, emitting only results that differ from the previous one. It is cold and starts per collector. It is the usual bridge from Compose state to Flow operators inside LaunchedEffect.
